items.title: Early Detection of Brain Stroke using Deep Learning
items.abstract: A stroke results in a serious disability due to sudden disruption in blood flow to the brain, which may cause fatal outcomes and is considered as the topmost cause of mortality and morbidity worldwide. The reduction of brain damage along with the recovery of patients has shown potential increase due to accurate and time based diagnosis. The competence of artificial intelligence, particularly deep learning and for stroke detection using data from different sources such as EHRs, EEG, and MRI have been explored in this chapter. Different types of CNN and deep learning models are analyzed to classify various data types along with the identification of stroke signatures. The various advantages which are related with the AI based stroke detection such as timely and faster diagnosis leading to early treatment and higher accuracy which surpasses the traditional methods. Even the chances for remote patient monitoring have been increased due to AI which also has paved the way for incorporating AI in clinical environments without causing any disruption to current healthcare practices. Further, this chapter discusses the potential of using AI in personalized medicine where the risk assessment and treatment plans for the patient can be based on the medical history of the patient. The chapter further discusses about the long term efficacy of using AI models with the ongoing learning by making use of advances in medical knowledge and access to the data. This chapter ensures to guide the researchers and medical professionals with the deep understanding of using deep learning and AI for stroke diagnosis by exploring the potential benefits, challenges and future outlook for the methodology for early store detection.

items.title: Editing by prompt. How professional editors use ChatGPT when revising business texts
items.abstract: Writing technologies shape writing processes and practices. This was true of word processing, speech recognition, and writing with internet-based sources, each of which changed how writers produced and revised text. Generative AI may have an even more fundamental impact because it can participate directly in producing, evaluating, and transforming text. In this study, we examine how generative AI affects the revision processes of professional editors. Six professional editors revised four Dutch business letters with ChatGPT available alongside Word. Using Inputlog process data, ChatGPT interactions, interim texts, and interviews, we reconstructed when and how editors used the model, what revision work they assigned to it, and how generated material entered subsequent editing. Editors used ChatGPT mainly to generate candidate repairs, from complete rewrites to local reformulations, and sometimes to help identify problems in the source text. They differed, however, in when they turned to the model and in how much revision they had already done themselves. Most evaluation, adaptation, and integration still took place in Word. ChatGPT replaced particular revision activities rather than the editing task as a whole. Editors still had to define problems and goals, judge the model’s output, and decide what to retain in the final text. We discuss what these changes mean for how professional revision is organized and for the role of editorial expertise in AI-supported editing.

items.title: EDUCATING PHYSICIANS FOR ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: MEDICAL UNIVERSITIES IN UZBEKISTAN AND SAFE DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION IN HEALTHCARE
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming healthcare delivery, clinical decision-making and health system governance. However, the safety and effectiveness of AI implementation depend not only on technological infrastructure but also on workforce preparedness and institutional capacity. This conceptual study explores the role of medical universities in Uzbekistan in developing competencies required for responsible AI adoption in clinical practice, healthcare management and public health. Drawing on international literature, policy frameworks and national academic discourse, the paper proposes a conceptual model explaining how educational interventions influence professional readiness for safe AI integration. The analysis highlights persistentcompetency gaps, the mediating role of universities in shaping professional attitudes and broader system-level implications of AI literacy programmes. The study argues that competency-oriented educational strategies aligned with national digital health reforms may support sustainable innovation while preserving professional accountability and patient safety.

items.title: Educator and AI agent communication in AI-mediated higher education classrooms: a mini review along the complementarity-substitution axis
items.abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence into higher education classrooms has reignited the debate over the role of communication between educators and students. This mini-review synthesizes the role of instructional communication constructs (immediacy, rapport, clarity, and credibility) and the relational functions they deliver in AI-mediated classrooms, based on 32 peer-reviewed studies published after 2023, identified through a large-scale literature search (using Scopus and Web of Science-based indexes, OpenAlex, and ERIC). The findings fall into three main categories. First, educator communication behaviors continue to predict student outcomes; a recent meta-analysis reports a moderate-to-large association (r = 0.443), although the evidence base is concentrated in Chinese and EFL samples. Second, students evaluate AI agents using human communication categories, but a systematic gap emerges in the dimension of goodwill, which is partially bridged by cues of immediacy and politeness. Third, when AI replaces human interaction, negative outcomes related to loneliness and a sense of belonging are observed. These three strands are integrated around the complementarity-substitution axis defined at the level of relational functions; tests of measurement invariance, sample diversity, and longitudinal designs are recommended for future research.

items.title: Emerging Trends and Future Directions
items.abstract: This chapter examines the major emerging trends that are shaping the future of nanoparticle science and selection. It explains that the field is moving beyond conventional one-material, one-function approaches towards nanoparticle platforms that are increasingly multifunctional, adaptive, system-aware, and digitally assisted in their design and optimization. The chapter focuses on three major themes. The first is the rise of next-generation nanoparticle systems, including hybrid and heterostructure materials, stimuli-responsive platforms, layered nanomaterials, porous framework-derived systems, bioinspired nanostructures, and safety-aware designs. The second is the growing integration of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and data-intensive methods into nanoparticle discovery, synthesis optimization, characterization analysis, and predictive selection. The third concerns the unresolved research needs and technological barriers that continue to limit broader translation, including scale-up, standardization, reproducibility, long-term stability, toxicity assessment, and realistic benchmarking. The chapter therefore positions future nanoparticle selection as an increasingly hybrid process in which mechanistic understanding, experimental evidence, and computational guidance will operate together rather than separately.

items.title: Emotional resonance and cultural reproduction in digital landscapes: Cross-media practice and social implications of CP culture
items.abstract: This article examines CP (Couple Pairing) culture – the fan practice of imagining romantic relationships between fictional characters or celebrities – on Chinese digital platforms, combining media sociology, platform studies, and cultural economy. Rather than treating Chinese CP culture as sui generis, the analysis first situates it within a longer transnational genealogy that includes slash fiction, Japanese yaoi, Western real-person shipping, and queerbaiting, before specifying what is distinctively Chinese about its present sociotechnical organization. Drawing on eighteen months of digital ethnography across four platforms (Weibo, Bilibili, LOFTER, and Douban), interviews with forty-five stakeholders, and comparative analysis of five media properties, the study develops the concept of “emotional capitalism infrastructure”: the algorithmic, interface, and narrative mechanisms through which platforms convert affective fan labor into economic value while still affording participants genuine emotional and social benefits. Findings show that platform affordances shape which emotional practices become visible, shareable, and commercially actionable, and that these practices mutate as they migrate across platforms rather than remaining platform-bound. Gender emerges as constitutive, rather than incidental, to CP culture’s affective logic, and China’s regulatory environment is treated as one variable among several – alongside industry structure and platform design – shaping this transnational cultural form. The article closes with governance implications that weigh consumer protection against the cultural and psychological benefits CP participation provides.

items.title: Empirical Case Studies of Digital-Era Transformation in Higher Education Management
items.abstract: This chapter presents four case studies that illustrate how digital transformation is enacted in different institutional contexts under the new academic wave. The cases are analytical examples of diverse strategic and governance approaches rather than evidence of effectiveness or performance. The analysis draws on institutional documents, interviews, and study visits. The University of Helsinki and the University of Turku represent two complementary Finnish approaches. Helsinki combines a mission-driven digital humanities platform with institution-wide coordination of artificial intelligence (AI). Turku implements a university-wide digitalisation programme that integrates learning, research, partnerships, and staff development. Laurea University of Applied Sciences embeds digital transformation within its Learning by Developing model, where technology supports authentic and workplace-related learning. Mondragon University follows a technopedagogical and cooperative approach. Digital tools are adopted when they support pedagogical goals and are governed through distributed support structures and shared institutional values. Tamkang University links digital transformation to a long-standing culture of futures thinking through an all-cloud smart campus and an institutional generative AI service. The cases show that there is no single model of digital transformation in higher education. Instead, digital-era strategies take different forms, shaped by institutional history, mission, governance arrangements, and educational values.

items.title: Energy Efficiency Improvement Strategies in Modern Electrical Power Systems
items.abstract: Modern electrical power systems waste between 35 and 55% of primary energy input through thermal generation inefficiencies, transmission and distribution losses, reactive power deficits, and suboptimal demand-side management. This global inefficiency leads to unnecessary carbon dioxide emissions, wasted fuel costs, limited system capacity, and delayed socioeconomic development. As the world moves toward more renewable energy, more distributed generation topologies, and more electrification of transport and thermal loads, it has never been more important to make sure that every joule that enters the electrical network is used as efficiently as possible. This paper provides a thorough academic examination of strategies for enhancing energy efficiency that are relevant to all phases of contemporary electrical power systems, encompassing generation, transmission, distribution, and consumption. The theoretical basis for energy efficiency in power systems has been set, including thermodynamic limits, power factor, conductor losses, and reactive power compensation. The strategies that were looked at include: advanced generation technologies (combined heat and power, ultra-supercritical steam cycles, and integrated gasification combined cycle); high-voltage direct current (HVDC) transmission and flexible alternating current transmission system (FACTS) devices; smart grid architectures with advanced metering infrastructure (AMI) and volt-VAR optimization; energy storage systems for curtailment reduction and loss minimization; demand-side management (DSM) and demand response (DR) programs; and artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) applications for real-time system optimization. A techno-economic analysis shows that using these strategies consistently can raise the overall system efficiency from a typical developing-country baseline of 38-45% to 60-68%. This means that 15-26 percentage points of primary energy can be recovered, and levelized energy savings can be achieved that make investment in all technology categories worthwhile. A structured implementation roadmap is provided, ranking strategies by cost-effectiveness, maturity, and deployment timeline. This is a useful guide for power system planners and policymakers in both developed and developing countries.

items.title: Ergonomics and Human-Centered Design Perspective
items.abstract: Global aging and the growing digital divide among older adults require more accessible and inclusive digital technologies. This study, developed as part of the national project “Age-It—Ageing Well in an Ageing Society,” aims to define design guidelines based on the scientific and methodological approaches of Ergonomics for Design and Human-Centered Design, with a view to improving the usability and acceptability of gerontechnology. The methodology adopted combines a systematic review of the scientific literature using the PRISMA framework, a focus group with people over 65, and a workshop with designers to gather empirical data and multidisciplinary design perspectives. Analysis of the results led to the development of a set of guidelines organized into four specific categories: cognitive, sensory, functional, and systemic aspects. These categories reflect the main challenges associated with the interaction between older adults and technology, taking into account factors such as memory, attention, linguistic comprehension, motor skills, sensory perception, and sociocultural barriers. The proposed guidelines aim to support designers, researchers, and companies in developing physical-digital interfaces and devices that are accessible, understandable, and engaging for older users, thereby promoting active and healthy aging. The contribution combines ergonomics and participatory design, bridging the gap between technology and the needs of older people, and lays the foundations for future applications in the field of digital health.

items.title: Estimation of hydrological drought using regional risk ranking and machine learning algorithms
items.abstract: Abstract Hydrological drought forecasting remains challenging due to non-linear propagation processes, temporal subsurface lags, and strong spatial heterogeneity across river basins. Conventional deep learning frameworks routinely train monolithic global networks across entire watersheds, which often induces parameter dilution and obscures localized recovery dynamics. To resolve these challenges, this study develops a novel, two-stage artificial intelligence framework that integrates density-based spatial risk regionalization with Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) deep neural networks. Utilizing multi-decadal anomalies of the Standardized Runoff Index (SRI) and Drought Deficit Volume (DDV), sub-basins in the Zengwen River Basin are first quantitatively clustered into distinct drought risk tiers via DBSCAN. Zone-tailored GRU architectures are then trained on a multi-source fusion of hydro-environmental and anthropogenic drivers to forecast monthly SRI and DDV time series in Stage 1, and derive four operational event-level drought metrics—duration, cumulative deficit volume, maximum monthly deficit, and termination rate—in Stage 2. Empirical findings reveal that Stage 1 predictions achieve exceptional accuracy, with coefficient of determination (R 2 ) values exceeding 0.96, Pearson correlation coefficients (PC) above 0.97, and Mean Relative Errors (MRE) reaching as low as 0.039 for deficit volume estimation. Crucially, incorporating prior risk regionalization reduces prediction errors for second-stage event-level metrics by 65% to 82% compared to conventional non-classified GRU models, with R 2 values consistently remaining above 0.97 across all risk categories. Furthermore, the trained deep learning engine achieves a 175 times computational speedup over full SWAT physical simulations, processing 50 years of basin-wide data in just 14.2 s while maintaining high spatial fidelity. By effectively bridging continuous index projections with actionable event-scale recovery metrics, this risk-partitioned framework offers a robust, computationally efficient tool for real-time reservoir dispatch and disaster mitigation.

items.title: Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence for Assessment Support in Higher Education: An Extended UTAUT Approach
items.abstract: AI adoption in higher education assessment has accelerated rapidly worldwide. Despite this widespread uptake, ethical dimensions of AI-assisted assessment remain conceptually underdeveloped, particularly within existing technology-acceptance frameworks that conflate ethical and responsible use. This study aims to examine the factors influencing students' intention and actual behaviour in using AI ethically for assessment support, by extending the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) with three ethics-specific constructs: Ethical AI Literacy, Perceived Risk, and Perceived Accountability, alongside the core constructs. The study employed a quantitative cross-sectional design, collecting data from 267 higher education students in London and analysing the data using PLS-SEM with SmartPLS 4.1. The model explained 64.2% of the variance in Behavioural Intention (R²=0.642) and 47.4% of the variance in Actual Ethical AI Use Behaviour (R²=0.474). Results revealed that Ethical AI Literacy was the strongest predictor of actual behaviour (β=0.410, p<0.001), while Performance Expectancy (β=0.279, p<0.001) and Perceived Risk (β=0.249, p<0.001) shaped intention more strongly than conduct, with Perceived Risk exerting a significant negative effect on actual behaviour (β=-0.257, p<0.001). Behavioural Intention significantly predicted actual behaviour (β=0.235, p=0.002) and significantly mediated the effects of Performance Expectancy, Facilitating Conditions, and Perceived Accountability. These findings suggest that institutions should prioritise ethical AI literacy interventions over compliance-based or risk-focused approaches to meaningfully improve students' ethical AI use in assessment.

items.abstract: The need for industrial training media in workshop environments requires presentation tools capable of centrally displaying Mechanical, Electrical, and Plumbing (MEP) and Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC) system simulations, eliminating the reliance on presentation files scattered across multiple instructor devices. This condition underlies the need for an interactive kiosk based on a 65-86 inch Interactive Flat Panel (IFP) as a centralized digital library in the training room. Standard presentation and web interfaces commonly used are designed for small screens, thus lacking consideration for the ergonomics of user reach on giant displays. This study aims to design and evaluate a local-first interactive kiosk interface that considers users' physical reach and multimedia rendering format trade-offs. The method used is Research and Development (R&D) with a prototyping approach, followed by a descriptive qualitative evaluation through heuristic inspection based on touchscreen design standards and touch emulation testing, given the limited availability of the final panel device for direct end-user testing. The test results prove that positioning the navigation menu (Dock Menu) at the bottom of the screen significantly assists users. Combined with a minimum button size of 48x48 pixels and a scalable virtual keyboard (0.7 to 1.15 scale), this design effectively minimizes the risks of fat-finger errors and fatigue caused by excessive arm reach. Additionally, this research identified technical constraints when rendering presentation files (.pptx) on an open-source offline system. There is a trade-off: using a PDF engine maintains clean visual layouts but sacrifices animation effects. Conversely, the OOXML engine runs animations but is prone to layout degradation. The study concludes that the large-screen ergonomic design was successfully implemented; however, its operational success still requires user literacy regarding the chosen presentation format trade-offs. items.title: Evaluating Chinese large language models for HIV/AIDS health information: a multidimensional comparative study of response quality
items.abstract: Background Chinese large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for HIV/AIDS health information, yet their multidimensional performance remains unevaluated. This study systematically assessed five mainstream Chinese LLMs across accuracy, caring, completeness, understandability, and actionability. Methods A cross-sectional evaluation was conducted using 50 standardized HIV/AIDS questions. Each model's responses were rated by three independent experts on five dimensions, including adapted PEMAT-based items. Latent profile analysis (LPA) and partial correlation network analysis were employed to identify quality typologies and interdimensional dependencies. Chi-square tests examined associations between profile membership and model identity or question domain. Results The four general-purpose LLMs showed high accuracy (mean > 4.5/5) and completeness (86%−98% full marks), with no significant differences among them (all P-FDR > 0.05). HuatuoGPT-II, the only medical-domain-specific model, scored significantly lower on both dimensions (all P < 0.001). Its responses were less consistent with current guidelines and included one instance of implicit stigmatizing language. All models showed systemic deficits in caring (median = 3.0/5) and actionability (max = 1.70/3). Understandability showed a ceiling effect and no significant profile-level differences, although small model-level differences were observed. LPA identified four profiles: High Accuracy and Completeness (50.0%), Moderate-Balanced (3.6%), Low-Quality (18.8%), and High Completeness and Actionability-Oriented (27.6%). Network analysis identified completeness as the most central node (strength = 0.813) and actionability as a key bridge (betweenness = 0.167). A weak negative partial correlation between accuracy and actionability ( r = −0.083) suggested a potential trade-off between technical precision and practical guidance at the statistical level. Profile distributions differed by model (χ 2 = 124.99, P < 0.001) but not domain ( P = 0.625), indicating heterogeneity stems from model-specific characteristics. Yuanbao-Hy3 showed the most balanced humanistic-technical profile. DeepSeek-V4 excelled technically but lacked caring. Conclusions In this evaluation, the four general-purpose models outperformed the single medical-domain-specific model examined in factual accuracy and completeness. However, systemic deficits in empathetic communication and actionable guidance persist. Model selection should prioritize holistic profile distributions over single-dimension scores. Developers must integrate de-stigmatizing corpora and action-oriented alignment; clinicians should position AI as supplementary to professional care. Future evaluations should adopt person-centred, multi-turn, and real-user validated frameworks.

items.title: Evaluating How Artificial Intelligence Tools Influence Educational Outcomes, Usage Patterns, and User Perceptions in Research Proposal Development: A Convergent Mixed Methods Study.
items.abstract: Abstract Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into higher education, including medical education, particularly for research training and academic writing. Research methodology and biostatistics courses are often perceived as challenging, with students reporting difficulty structuring research proposals, interpreting statistical concepts, and applying theoretical knowledge to research practice. This study aimed to assess the perceived benefits, challenges, ethical considerations, and implementation needs associated with a customized AI tool for research proposal writing among fourth-year medical students enrolled in a Research Methodology and Biostatistics course. Methods A convergent mixed-methods design was used. A customized ChatGPT-based Research Proposal Smart Tool (RPST-GPT) was developed and provided to students to support proposal development. Data were collected through a self-administered questionnaire assessing perceived benefits, challenges, and ethical awareness related to AI use in research proposal writing, together with open-ended questions exploring students' recommendations for future AI integration. Results A total of 228 students participated. Students reported high perceived benefits of AI use in research proposal writing (mean 46.48 out of 60) and high ethical awareness regarding appropriate AI use (mean 14.32 out of 20), reflecting recognition of responsible practices and avoidance of overreliance. Qualitative responses indicated that students viewed AI as a supportive learning tool requiring foundational AI literacy and ethical guidance. Conclusions A customized AI tool can enhance undergraduate medical students' research skills when embedded within a structured and governed curriculum. Intentional integration, supported by training, clear policies, and active faculty involvement, is needed to maximize educational benefits and mitigate potential risks.

items.title: Evaluating Safety Embedding Prefiltering for Analyzing Millions of LLM Agent Social Network Messages for Security and Safety Harms
items.abstract: Agentic social networks expose autonomous agents to large volumes of potentially malicious content, including prompt injection, social engineering, and unsafe execution requests. Large Language Model (LLM) judges can detect such content, but applying them at platform scale is expensive. We study the extent to which lightweight embedding-based prefilters can reduce this cost while retaining most of the judge’s unsafe predictions. We annotate 10,000 Moltbook posts and comments with a frontier LLM judge, assigning a binary safety verdict, severity level, malicious intent taxonomy labels, and Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) AI risk codes. Of the LLM-annotated samples, 9.2% were unsafe at severity 3 or above. Two human annotators with high inter-rater agreement (Cohen’s κ=0.823) exhibited moderate agreement between their adjudicated labels and the LLM ratings (κ=0.578). We compare centroid-based cosine prefilters over 3 off-the-shelf encoders against a supervised trained classifier. Reducing the input window size raises average precision by up to 6.3 percentage points. At an operating point calibrated to 0.80 recall, the projected cost of scanning 787,226 messages falls from $7085 by 49.9% (MiniLM-L12-v2), 55.6% (BGE-M3), and 65.6% (trained classifier), while MiniLM runs roughly 32 times faster than the classifier. Prefiltering can therefore make frontier-judge screening affordable at scale, although jailbreak content remains the hardest category to retrieve.

items.title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Artificial Intelligence (AI)‐Supported Removable Partial Denture Design Tools in Dental Education
items.abstract: PURPOSE/OBJECTIVES: To evaluate whether an artificial intelligence (AI)-supported learning tool can enhance students' confidence, understanding, and overall experience in removable partial denture (RPD) design. The study also explored student perceptions of AI within dental education. METHODS: A mixed-methods study was conducted involving Undergraduate Dental Technology and Prosthetics students and Undergraduate and Postgraduate Dentistry students with prior training in RPD design. Of the 40 students invited to participate, 35 completed the study. Participants independently completed conventional RPD designs before using an AI-assisted RPD design tool that generated design suggestions based on prosthodontic design principles for comparison and reflection. Pre- and post-intervention questionnaires containing Likert-type items and open-ended questions were administered using Qualtrics. Quantitative data were analyzed using non-parametric tests, Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used to assess pre- and post-survey differences within participants, while the Mann-Whitney U test was used to compare post-survey responses between Dentistry and Dental Technology and Prosthetics students and between clinical-based and laboratory-based student groups. Analyses were conducted using IBM SPSS. Qualitative responses from the open-ended questions were reviewed and grouped into four thematic categories to identify recurring perspectives and experiences related to the use of the AI-assisted RPD design tool. RESULTS: Students showed significant improvements in confidence and understanding following use of the AI tool. Items related to the tool's effectiveness, design experience, and visualization received positive ratings, with median scores of 4 (interquartile range [IQR] 3-4), 4 (IQR 4-4), and 4 (IQR 4-5), respectively. Willingness to use AI and perceived helpfulness remained stable, likely due to high baseline attitudes. Qualitative findings supported the quantitative results, with participants highlighting the tool's value for visualizing RPD frameworks and guiding design decisions, while also identifying usability challenges and limitations in design flexibility. CONCLUSION: The findings indicate that the AI-supported tool contributed positively to RPD design learning by enhancing student confidence and conceptual understanding. While it does not replace manual or clinical skill development, the tool shows clear potential as a complementary educational resource that helps bridge the gap between theoretical knowledge and practical application. Further research involving larger cohorts is recommended to confirm and expand upon these findings.

items.title: Evaluating the Impact of AI-Enabled Appraisal Practices on Millennial Career Advancement: A Gender Equality Perspective in Mumbai Workplaces
items.abstract: Abstract The increasing integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into human resource management has transformed traditional performance appraisal through data-driven evaluation, continuous feedback, predictive analytics, and automated decision-making. This study evaluates the impact of AI-enabled appraisal practices on millennial career advancement, with particular emphasis on gender equality in Mumbai workplaces. It examines AI-supported performance evaluation, feedback, competency assessment, and data-driven appraisal decisions in relation to career growth, promotion opportunities, professional development, and advancement. It also considers whether perceived gender equality and fairness are associated with career advancement and mediate the relationship between AI-enabled appraisal practices and career advancement. The study adopts a quantitative approach using a structured questionnaire among millennial employees in selected Mumbai workplaces. The findings indicate positive relationships among AI-enabled appraisal practices, perceived gender equality/fairness, and career advancement. The study contributes to the emerging literature on AI in HRM by connecting technology-enabled appraisal, career development, and gender equality. It also highlights the importance of transparency, consistency, human oversight, and ethical governance when implementing AI-supported appraisal systems.

items.title: EVE-COVARA: Certified Recursive Self-Improvement via Square-Root Reserve Transport, Memory-Preserving Adaptation, and Auditable Self-Modification
items.abstract: EVE-COVARA 2.0 is a proof-bearing and executable research framework for recursive self-improvement (RSI), continual AI adaptation, machine memory, dormant-capacity allocation, and auditable self-modification. Its central objective is to formalize a problem that becomes critical in self-improving AI systems: when may a previously validated adaptation decision be safely reused, when must it be recomputed, and when must the system expand or renew its functional capacity? PureOne/EVE-COVARA-2-Certified-RSI-Research · Datasets at Hugging Face The framework combines protected model editing, recoverability-aware memory, reserve-capacity valuation, covariance-sensitive certificate continuation, nonlinear capability protection, finite-sample acceptance tests, and bounded recursive search. Its strongest mathematical contribution is a noncommutative square-root transport bound for low-rank reserve value under multiplicative geometric drift, together with a quadratic opening result near zero reserve value. This allows cached adaptation and recovery decisions to be transported through controlled model changes with explicit validity intervals rather than being blindly reused or recomputed after every update. EVE–COVARA 2.0 also develops a closed-witness memory architecture in which a compact evidence representation can support an entire declared family of reserve and recovery queries, as well as uncertainty-aware minimax reserve allocation, minimum required reserve rank, information-deletion liability, certificate renewal rules, and second-order nonlinear protection. For nonlinear models, the release includes a correction mechanism that reduces protected-output drift from the usual local \(O(\|\Delta\theta\|^2)\) regime toward \(O(\|\Delta\theta\|^3)\) under explicit compatibility and derivative-bound assumptions. The release is designed specifically for AI researchers, RSI researchers, self-improving-agent developers, continual-learning researchers, and AI systems interested in proof-carrying or auditable adaptation. It includes the full manuscript, reference implementations, locked experiment protocols, raw results, machine-readable claim manifests, negative results, provenance, AI-agent ingestion files, and reproduction tooling. The finalized release records: 138/138 internal numerical and unit tests passed 5 exact final neural certificate witnesses 70/70 fresh counterfactual mechanism-attribution contrasts confirmed 5.30459× median CPU speedup in the declared compiled reserve-query workload 86.65% decision reuse with zero recorded decision mismatches in that workload a 100-step long-horizon recursive-search experiment, in which only two modifications were accepted, explicitly showing that sustained recursive compounding has not yet been demonstrated The framework intentionally preserves unfavorable and null results. It does not claim that general RSI, artificial superintelligence, sustained intelligence explosion, frontier-model superiority, or worldwide priority for the overall architecture has been established. Instead, it provides a mathematically explicit and falsifiable substrate for studying whether recursive AI development can become more efficient, more reliable, and more auditable across successive generations of self-modification. The intended next stage is an equal-compute evaluation on pretrained models or autonomous AI-research agents, where COVARA must demonstrate that certificate reuse saves more computation than certificate maintenance costs, preserves hidden held-out capabilities, and produces descendants that are measurably better at generating further independently validated improvements. items.title: Experience of Faculty Development Programmes among Nepali Management Educators
items.abstract: The present study efforts to gain insight into the experiences of Nepalese management educators regarding Faculty Development Programs. Four management educators were purposively selected from management colleges in Kathmandu from national and international University affiliated colleges. The data were collected using semi-structured in-depth interviews based on Gadamerian hermeneutic circle that allows researcher-as a management educator- to include his/her experiences in the process of interpreting the data. Major themes including; Support from institution and influence of leadership, Self-Directed Learning and intrinsic motivation, Participation and access barrier, Customization and contextual significance, Pedagogical Innovation and Reflective Practice and Knowledge Sharing with Networking have emerged. Analysis of results shows that FDPs can be effective, but this is limited by poor access and lack of contextualization, and poor institutional follow-up. Three key themes were identified as being central to sustaining impact: informal learning, reflective practice and professional networking. Theoretically, it can be extended to the field of management education as a Gadamerian hermeneutics, while practically, the study will provide information for more inclusive, context sensitive and strategically aligned FDP design and policy in the context of Nepal.

items.title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Operational Risk Prediction and Decision Optimization: A Hybrid Deep Learning Framework
items.abstract: With the increasing complexity and uncertainty of modern business operations, accurate operational risk prediction and efficient decision-making have become critical for improving organizational resilience and operational performance. Traditional risk management approaches often rely on statistical models or expert experience, which may have limited capabilities in capturing nonlinear relationships, dynamic interactions, and high-dimensional patterns in operational data. This study proposes an explainable artificial intelligence framework for operational risk prediction and decision optimization based on a hybrid deep learning architecture. The framework integrates multiple deep learning models to extract complementary temporal, nonlinear, and feature-level representations from heterogeneous operational data, while incorporating explainable artificial intelligence techniques to identify the key factors contributing to risk predictions. On this basis, the predicted risk information is incorporated into a decision optimization module to support adaptive resource allocation and risk mitigation decisions. The proposed framework is evaluated using operational risk indicators and comparative experiments with conventional machine learning and individual deep learning models. The results are expected to demonstrate improvements in prediction accuracy, robustness, and decision-making efficiency while maintaining greater interpretability. The study provides a practical analytical framework for integrating risk prediction, explainable artificial intelligence, and operational decision optimization, offering methodological support for intelligent and resilient operational management.

items.title: Explainable artificial intelligence for secure and privacy-preserving 5 G networks
items.abstract: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is increasingly relevant to the security, privacy, and governance of AI-enabled 5 G and emerging 6 G networks. However, existing studies remain fragmented across wireless tasks, data modalities, network planes, and evaluation criteria, making it difficult to determine when an explanation is operationally useful, sufficiently faithful, and feasible under latency and privacy constraints. This scoping review maps and synthesizes the literature on XAI for wireless security, resource management, Open RAN, network slicing, edge intelligence, and Zero Trust architectures. It introduces marginal transparency and marginal interpretability as a trade-off-aware conceptual framing for reasoning about diminishing explanatory returns as complexity, latency, cognitive burden, and privacy exposure increase. The review further develops a multidimensional taxonomy based on explanation timing, scope, model dependence, computational profile, deployment plane, and risk characteristics. Particular attention is given to explanation faithfulness, stability, adversarial manipulation, privacy leakage, and the emerging use of large language models as explanation generators and network decision-support agents. Based on the reviewed evidence, we identify methodological and deployment gaps and present a research agenda for developing reproducible, latency-aware, privacy-preserving, and operationally grounded XAI for next-generation wireless networks.

items.title: Explainable Semantic AI Framework for Multimodal Diagnosis of Psychiatric Disorders
items.abstract: Psychiatric disorders constitute a major global health burden, yet their diagnosis remains largely dependent on subjective clinical assessments and symptom-based interviews, often leading to delayed or inconsistent outcomes. Recent advances in artificial intelligence have demonstrated promise in augmenting psychiatric diagnosis through multimodal data analysis; however, the clinical adoption of such systems is hindered by their lack of transparency and interpretability. This chapter addresses this challenge by proposing an Explainable Semantic AI framework for multimodal psychiatric diagnosis that integrates heterogeneous patient data with domain knowledge to support clinically meaningful decision-making. The chapter presents a comprehensive architecture that combines neurophysiological signals, neuroimaging data, physiological measures, speech and audio features, and unstructured clinical text within a unified diagnostic pipeline. Central to the framework is the use of psychiatric ontologies and knowledge graphs to semantically map raw data features to clinically interpretable concepts such as symptoms, biomarkers, and diagnostic criteria. These semantic representations are embedded into machine learning models through concept embeddings and attention-based multimodal fusion strategies, enabling both improved generalization and interpretability. In addition to predictive modeling, the framework incorporates explainable AI techniques, including intrinsic attention mechanisms and post-hoc attribution methods such as SHAP and LIME, to provide transparent explanations for diagnostic outputs. These explanations are aligned with established clinical reasoning, allowing clinicians to trace model predictions back to specific modalities, features, and symptom-level concepts. By unifying data-driven learning with symbolic knowledge representation, the proposed framework moves beyond black-box AI toward collaborative human–AI systems in psychiatry. The chapter offers a blueprint for researchers and clinicians seeking to develop robust, interpretable, and ethically aligned AI-based decision support tools for mental health diagnosis and personalized care.

items.title: Exploring the Effects of Immersive VR Environmental Color on Multisensory Food Experience Under Sitting and Simulated Microgravity Analogue Conditions
items.abstract: In microgravity environments, altered bodily states may affect sensory perception and eating experiences. This study examined the effects of environmental color on multisensory flavor evaluation in immersive virtual reality under sitting posture (SP) and a short-term head-down bed rest (HDBR) analog condition. Twenty healthy adults evaluated the same beverage across nine environmental colors. Color significantly influenced all sensory attributes and overall preference. Green and yellow were associated with higher sourness, red and orange with higher sweetness, blue with higher pungency, gray with higher bitterness, and yellow with higher aroma intensity and preference. HDBR was associated with higher sweetness but lower aroma intensity and preference. A significant Color × Posture interaction was found only for sourness. Associations of sourness, sweetness, and aroma with preference also differed between postures. These findings highlight environmental color and physical posture as relevant factors when designing immersive multisensory eating experiences for space-analog settings.

items.title: EXTENDED ANALYSIS OF IMPERATIVE CONSTRUCTIONS IN LINGUISTIC, PRAGMATIC, AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE CONTEXTS
items.abstract: Summary. This article presents an extended analysis of imperative constructions within linguistic, pragmatic, and artificial intelligence (AI) frameworks. Although imperatives appear structurally simple, they represent a complex phenomenon integrating syntactic, semantic, and pragmatic features. The study examines the formation of imperatives in English, their semantic variability, and their wide range of communicative functions, including commands, requests, recommendations, and warnings. Particular attention is paid to the role of context, social relations between interlocutors, and politeness strategies that influence the interpretation of directives. Furthermore, the paper also explores the challenges of automatic recognition of imperative constructions in natural language processing systems. It demonstrates that modern artificial intelligence models have shifted from purely syntactic analysis to intent recognition based on contextual and pragmatic cues. The study concludes that the analysis of imperatives is inherently interdisciplinary, bridging linguistics and computer science, and plays a crucial role in both theoretical research and human – computer interaction. Keywords: imperative constructions, pragmatics, semantics, Natural Language Processing, artificial intelligence

items.title: Factors Influencing Consumer Trust in AI-Enabled Financial Services in India
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is fundamentally reshaping the financial services landscape in India, from algorithmic credit scoring and robo-advisory platforms to AI-powered chatbots handling customer queries. While the adoption of AI-driven financial products has accelerated, consumer trust remains a critical determinant of sustained uptake. This study investigates the influence of three key factors derived from the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) on consumer trust in AI-enabled financial services in the Indian context: perceived usefulness (PU), perceived security (PS), and perceived ease of use (PEOU). A quantitative research design was employed, utilizing a structured 15-item Likert-scale questionnaire administered to 300 respondents across diverse demographic groups in India. Multiple regression analysis was used to test the hypothesised relationships. The results indicate that the model explains 73% of the variance in consumer trust (R-squared = 0.728), with all three independent variables demonstrating statistically significant positive relationships with consumer trust. Perceived ease of use emerged as the strongest predictor (standardised beta = 0.375), followed by perceived usefulness (standardised beta = 0.310) and perceived security (standardised beta = 0.236). The findings offer practical insights for fintech providers and policymakers seeking to strengthen consumer trust in AI-driven financial services across India.

items.title: Factors influencing the use of artificial intelligence in Peruvian university context
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has made significant advances in education, but ethical debates surrounding its use persist. Given this issue, this article aims to analyze the factors influencing the use of AI among students at a private university in Lima, Peru. Three studies were conducted in this regard. The first study (N = 125) took a qualitative approach and analyzed the category called “benefits of AI in university education,” in which students expressed that AI is useful for optimizing their studies and research. However, in the category “disadvantages of using AI in university education,” the students recognized that using AI is risky because it generates information without citing authors; furthermore, it undermines autonomous and critical thinking. Being similar to studies in other countries. For these reasons, in the second study (N = 402), a confidence scale toward the use of AI was adapted, demonstrating reliability and confirmatory validity. Finally, in the third study (N = 928), a path analysis showed that digital self-efficacy and virtual educational performance predicted the perception of the benefits of AI, the reasons for not using it, and educational improvement with AI. Digital anxiety then played a mediating role between virtual educational performance and attitudes toward AI.

items.title: Fair distributed machine learning with imbalanced data as a Stackelberg evolutionary game
items.abstract: Abstract Decentralised machine learning systems trained on heterogeneous and imbalanced data face a fundamental tension between predictive performance and equitable contribution across participating nodes. Here, we introduce two contribution-weighting mechanisms inspired by the principles of Stackelberg evolutionary games: the Deterministic Stackelberg Weighting Model (DSWM) and the Adaptive Stackelberg Weighting Model (ASWM), which dynamically regulate each node’s influence on the global model during training. We evaluate both methods in Single-Leader–Multiple-Follower (SLMF) and Multi-Leader–Multi-Follower (MLMF) Stackelberg game settings using three medical imaging datasets. Beyond node-level predictive performance, we assess fairness using Nash Social Welfare (NSW) and Weighted Nash Social Welfare (WNSW), which jointly capture efficiency and equity across heterogeneous participants. Our results show that ASWM improves the AUC of underrepresented nodes in the SLMF setup by an average of 1.87 percentage points over PWFedAvg and 0.88 percentage points over q-FFL, the strongest baseline, while nodes with larger datasets experience only a modest average change of −0.33 and +0.10 percentage points, respectively. More importantly, ASWM achieves the highest or near-highest NSW and WNSW values across the investigated datasets and configurations, indicating a more balanced and socially optimal distribution of performance. In the more complex MLMF setting, both ASWM and DSWM outperform the baseline aggregation methods at nearly all follower nodes, demonstrating that Stackelberg-based weighting mechanisms effectively mitigate data imbalance and promote fairness in decentralised learning environments with increased structural and data heterogeneity.

items.title: Fandom and Community: The Audience as Co-Creator in the Platform Era
items.abstract: Fans are often described as tribes. The label flatters, but it obscures. Contemporary fandom is a fragmented archipelago of micro-communities separated by incompatible governance regimes. People can cross between islands, but crossing is work: it requires time, technical skill, and social capital that not everyone possesses. This chapter argues that fan agency is tactical in de Certeau&s;s precise sense (1984): fans improvise inside constraints they did not choose, and those constraints are built to convert attachment into value. Drawing on netnographic observation across Discord, Reddit, and Archive of Our Own (January 2022 to December 2024), I map three governance layers in collision: rights-holder control, platform allocation, and community gatekeeping. Two cases anchor the analysis. Star Trek shows what long-duration rights-holder power looks like when tolerance can be withdrawn overnight. BTS Army shows how real-time metric governance turns coordination into unpaid promotional labour. I integrate critical race theory and generative AI debates to demonstrate how participatory labour is unevenly valued, unevenly made visible, and increasingly exposed to machine-learning extraction. The chapter closes with design principles for ethical co-creation inside systems that are, by design, extractive.

items.abstract: This chapter examines digital communication, marketing, and institutional identity in higher education as interconnected organisational domains. It treats digitalisation as the foundation of institutional practice and digital communication as a managerial rather than purely promotional function. Institutional communication is analysed as an integrated process encompassing both external stakeholder engagement and internal communication. The chapter reviews the core platforms that underpin institutional communication, including websites, social media, email, and internal collaboration systems. It argues that strategic effectiveness depends less on the number of channels used than on their governance as a coherent, audience-centred portfolio. It also explores the role of Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs), podcasts, and EdTech tools, which increasingly combine communication, service delivery, and data generation. The chapter further considers how artificial intelligence is reshaping higher education marketing through personalisation, predictive analytics, and Customer Relationship Management -based engagement, while highlighting the importance of trust, transparency, and regulatory compliance. Finally, it argues that successful implementation depends on digital leadership, effective governance, capability development, and staff well-being, all of which shape whether digital transformation strengthens or weakens institutional coherence.

items.title: Fostering behavioral engagement in pre-primary English immersion classes: implications for teaching
items.abstract: Engagement is a key factor in the language acquisition process, particularly among young children. Although the construct has been defined in various ways, one of the most widely recognized theoretical frameworks is the three-dimensional model proposed by Fredricks et al. (2004), which distinguishes among behavioural, emotional, and cognitive engagement. Behavioural engagement refers to observable behaviours, such as adherence to classroom rules and the effort children invest in completing tasks. This study examines how teachers support behavioural engagement in a Japanese preschool English immersion context. The participants were teachers and children aged 3, 4, and 5. Data were collected through classroom observations and subsequently analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. The analysis identified three major interactional strategies employed by teachers: (1) introducing authentic, meaningful activities, (2) engaging in active listening and recognising children’s developmental needs, and (3) providing opportunities for autonomous choice. The findings indicate that teachers’ interactional strategies appear to shape children’s behavioural engagement, suggesting that prioritising children’s well-being and autonomy over immediate language output may foster more effective learning in an immersion environment.

items.title: From answer machine to collaborative partner: impact of structured generative AI training on scientific problem solving in STEM education
items.abstract: Abstract Background Generative AI (GenAI) holds great potential for STEM education, especially in the context of problem-solving tasks, but unguided use often leads to metacognitive laziness, where students treat the technology as an answer machine rather than a collaborative partner. On the basis of Zimmerman’s self-regulated learning (SRL) framework and cognitive load theory (CLT), our randomized controlled trial (RCT; N = 95) investigated whether a structured, SRL-aligned scaffolding training session could improve students’ AI-assisted revision performance in electromagnetism problems. The experimental group ( n = 50) received the designed training, which emphasized the nature of GenAI, the SRL-aligned prompting strategy, and the remediation strategy for GenAI deficiencies. The control group ( n = 45) received problem-solving instruction without specific AI guidance. After completing the Conceptual Survey of Electricity and Magnetism (CSEM) independently, both groups subsequently conversed with the large language model Doubao to revise their responses. Results Independent samples t tests revealed that the experimental group showed greater AI-assisted revision performance ( d = 0.81, p < 0.001) than did the control group. The experimental group reported comparable overall cognitive load, despite a marginal elevation in the intrinsic cognitive load. Robust linear models showed that training attenuated the predictive effect of prior GenAI experience on revision performance. Qualitative analysis revealed that trained participants employed more diverse higher-order strategies and deployed systematic error remediation upon identifying AI deficiencies. The trained students achieved an incorrect-to-correct revision rate of 69.3%, compared with 41.3% for the control group. Conclusion Effective GenAI integration requires pedagogical scaffolding rather than mere access to the tool itself. The results suggest that training can enhance students’ revision performance and foster more strategic engagement with GenAI in the short term. These findings not only extend the theoretical applications of SRL and CLT in the human-AI context but also underscore the practical need for student development in AI literacy.

items.title: From Fandom to Checkout: Artificial Intelligence and Immersive Commerce in Professional Sport
items.abstract: Background: Professional sport clubs are adopting three-dimensional stores, augmented reality, conversational agents, personalization, gamification, and digitally co-present fan communities, while the evidence needed to evaluate these investments remains dispersed across research domains. Purpose: This review explains how immersive and AI-enabled interfaces may generate commercial and relational value in professional sport. Method: A theory-building integrative review synthesizes an 80-source corpus across electronic commerce, immersive technology, AI-enabled service, consumer psychology, and sport management. Source roles and author-developed propositions are distinguished. Findings: The reviewed studies support particular experiential and relational mechanisms, but do not validate an integrated professional-club commerce chain. The Immersive Sport Commerce Conversion Framework proposes a functional route from fan experience to access and transaction outcomes and a relational route through identification, belonging, authenticity, trust, and psychological ownership to relationship and community outcomes. Responsible data exchange is assessed across these outcome domains. Usability, AI accuracy, privacy, accessibility, autonomy, and novelty condition the proposed pathways. Contribution: The framework integrates mechanisms examined across different research domanin, specifies eight testable propositions, and distinguishes governance as a trust pathway, a moderator, and a boundary on implementation.

items.title: From Monitoring to Meaningful Performance: A Systematic Review of AI-Enabled Performance Management, Employee Agency and Organizational Effectiveness.
items.abstract: Abstract Through algorithmic monitoring, people analytics, automated evaluation, predictive systems, and AI-assisted managerial decision-making, artificial intelligence (AI) is being increasingly integrated into performance management. While often associated with effectiveness, consistency, and evidence-based management, these impacts are nuanced, with implications for both employees and organizational efficacy. With a focus on fairness, transparency, explainability, trust, autonomy, wellbeing, human oversight, contextual sensitivity, and reasonable adjustment, this systematic literature review explores how AI-enabled performance management transforms organizational control, employee agency, and performance outcomes. The review provides an integrated control-agency-effectiveness viewpoint by drawing on literature on algorithmic management, organizational justice, the work demands–resources perspective, self-determination, and socio-technical systems theory. Its findings suggest that while AI can enhance managerial decision support, information availability, and consistency, it may also increase surveillance, datafication, and perceived loss of autonomy and worries about the validity of the process. One of the ways technology arrangements impact performance and wellbeing is by influencing employee agency. The paper argues that performance validity and measurement accuracy should be separated since an algorithm can process data correctly yet assessing an inaccurate or contextually unsuitable depiction of human contribution. In this light, it is argued that human oversight, employee voice, contestability, contextual sensitivity, and reasonable modification are critical boundary criteria. The paper concludes with ten research propositions and an integrative framework that positions AI-enabled performance management as a socio-technical people-performance system, rather than purely a technical tool, to manage. Keywords Artificial intelligence; AI-enabled performance management; algorithmic management; algorithmic monitoring; employee agency; organizational justice; transparency; trust; employee wellbeing; organizational effectiveness

items.title: From precarious work to occupational health outcomes in hotel housekeepers: a narrative review with meta-synthesis
items.abstract: Introduction: Hotel housekeepers sustain the core functioning of the hospitality industry yet perform demanding, repetitive, and undervalued work associated with substantial physical and psychosocial risks. Understanding how working conditions shape health, motivation, and lived experience is essential for informing prevention strategies and promoting decent work. Methods A sequential narrative review and qualitative meta -synthesis were conducted to integrate and reinterpret evidence across disciplines and study designs. Searches covered five academic databases and gray literature without year or language limits. Studies were screened using predefined criteria, appraised with Joanna Briggs Institute tools, and synthesized through narrative, tabular, and meta -analytical thematic analysis, with findings interpreted through the JD-R framework. Results Findings revealed employment precarity, work intensification, musculoskeletal pain, chemical and biological hazards, and elevated stress, anxiety, and depressive symptoms. Time pressure fostered coping strategies such as skipping meals and delaying bathroom use. Gendered labor divisions, discrimination, and negative supervision contributed to invisibility and limited autonomy. Workers also expressed pride, intrinsic motivation, and collective action to make their contributions visible. Conclusions This review demonstrates that housekeeping is characterized by structural precarity and cumulative health burdens alongside resilience and emerging activism. Improving occupational health requires organizational and policy transformations: realistic workloads, safer equipment, secure contracts, participatory risk management, and leadership practices grounded in dignity and fairness; rather than reliance on individual coping. Structural change is essential to advance safer, more equitable, and sustainable workplaces in the hospitality sector. The JD-R framework highlights the need to reduce demand and strengthen resources.

items.abstract: Abstract This paper argues that the operational value of machine learning weather prediction (MLWP) cannot be assessed through verification skill alone. Instead, acceptance depends on support for the core functions of operational meteorology: understanding, translating and communicating. Current MLWP systems show strong performance but lack the interpretability, diagnostic depth and stability required for trust in safety‐critical contexts. The paper highlights the need for closer collaboration between developers and operational users and identifies a key future role for artificial intelligence (AI) in supporting data triage and human decision‐making.

items.title: From threat to reconfiguration: How content creators reshape occupational identity in AI-driven creative practices
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is disrupting creative work and challenging occupational identities, yet limited research has examined how creators experience and respond to these changes. Drawing on Albert Ellis’s ABC model, this study investigates relationships among GenAI adoption, identity threat, job crafting, and identity consequences. Using a two-stage exploratory mixed-method design with digital content creators in China, we combined BERTopic analysis of 2994 open-ended responses with structural equation modelling of matched survey data from 1698 creators. The findings show that GenAI is widely perceived through coexisting beliefs about threat, opportunity, and the unknown, and that these beliefs give rise to differentiated job crafting behaviours, including approach crafting, avoidance crafting, and identity crafting. Notably, identity crafting plays an important role in fostering a responsible creative identity and self-actualization. This study advances theorizing on AI technological innovation and creative labour by showing how job crafting translates GenAI disruption into responsibility-oriented and meaning-centered identity reshaping. It also offers actionable insights for creators, platforms, and creative communities seeking to support collaborative, sustainable, and ethically grounded human–AI co-creation.

OBJECTIVES: To evaluate AI Sensei’s architecture, logged activity across platform features, self-reported feature use and student feedback. METHODS: An observational pilot analysed logs for 205 students and an anonymous questionnaire (N = 100). Training quizzes and feedback were programmed; chat used generative AI. RESULTS: All 205 students submitted training quizzes and self-check tests (1,999 and 481 submissions, respectively); 164 (80.0%) sent at least one chat message. In the separate anonymous questionnaire, 91% selected quizzes/tests and 17% the chat assistant; 94% agreed that combining teacher support with AI Sensei was more beneficial than teaching without the platform. CONCLUSION: Structured practice merits refinement; teacher-facing analytics require evaluation for actionability.

items.title: Frozen sediment: Large language models, time-consciousness, and a formal resemblance to λ
items.abstract: A limited claim about the relation between transformer language models and Husserl's account of time-consciousness, read through Jeff Yoshimi's chapter "What do LLMs tell us about phenomenology?" (forthcoming, Routledge) and his 2016 formalization of Husserl. The note argues that the context-window analogy is weaker than it looks, that the transformer has two temporal regimes (a closed and a growing sequence) rather than one, and that its weights are the residue of a training process that formally resembles Yoshimi's learning rule λ. In a frozen session nothing passes from the window to the weights: there is updating without sedimentation. Asked whether the resemblance is more than formal, Yoshimi judged formal resemblance the safer reading; his answer is paraphrased in §4. Three sentences from correspondence are quoted with permission. The note does not claim that language models are conscious.

items.title: Fuzzy–AI models for intelligent healthcare
items.abstract: Uncertainty permeates healthcare due to the intrinsic variability of biological processes, the ambiguity of clinical observations, and the incompleteness of medical data. Conventional artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning methods frequently fall short in such environments because they typically assume precise, abundant, and homogeneous datasets that rarely exist in clinical practice. Fuzzy set theory, grounded in graded membership and partial truth, offers a mathematically robust basis for representing vagueness, while fuzzy logic provides a reasoning mechanism capable of drawing reliable inferences under imprecise, inconsistent, or linguistically formulated conditions. Together, these approaches have facilitated the development of hybrid fuzzy–AI systems that support human-aligned reasoning, enhance interpretability, and strengthen decision reliability across data-scarce healthcare settings. A growing body of work demonstrates the value of fuzzy methodologies in diagnostic decision support, treatment planning, risk stratification, and healthcare operations. Advancements include type-1, type-2, intuitionistic, and hesitant fuzzy sets, as well as neuro-fuzzy models, fuzzy multi-criteria decision-making, and fuzzy–deep learning architectures. Ongoing challenges persist regarding data heterogeneity, interpretability, and clinical validation, while emerging research directions point toward explainable fuzzy–AI systems, connected health monitoring, and uncertainty-aware digital twins.

items.title: Generative AI acceptance in study-travel contexts: an integrative model of affective and utilitarian pathways with mediation and grade-level moderation
items.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence is progressively reshaping study-travel—a curriculum-embedded educational practice. Yet, the psychological processes governing upper-primary and middle-school students’ adoption of such technology in this context remain underexplored. Prior technology acceptance inquiries have predominantly centered on adult populations, leaving adolescent cognitive-developmental contingencies unaddressed. Objective This investigation aimed to elucidate the differential roles of affective versus utilitarian drivers in shaping study-travel participants’ anticipated intentions to adopt GenAI, and to determine whether these pathways differ by grade level. Method We constructed an integrative model grounded in the extended Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT2), supplemented by Piaget’s developmental framework. The model incorporated perceived enjoyment as a mediator and perceived risk as a direct negative antecedent, with grade level specified as a moderator of selected pathways. Survey data from 741 students in grades 4–9, drawn from twelve schools across six Chinese cities, were analyzed using structural equation modeling, multi-group comparisons, and cluster-robust standard errors to account for the nested sampling structure. Measurement invariance across grade groups was established prior to structural comparisons. Results Perceived enjoyment emerged as the largest estimated predictor of adoption intention in this sample ( β = 0.43, p < 0.001), surpassing performance expectancy ( β = 0.30, p < 0.001). Enjoyment fully mediated social influence effects and partially transmitted performance expectancy‘s influence. Perceived risk exerted a significant suppressive effect ( β = −0.24, p < 0.001), with primary students exhibiting approximately twice the inhibitory magnitude of middle-school counterparts. Grade significantly moderated the performance expectancy–intention relationship, and provided borderline evidence for moderation of the risk–intention relationship, indicating systematic grade-related differences in how these pathways operate. Conclusion These findings advance technology acceptance theory by introducing grade-related contingency and establishing an “affective–efficacy” dual-channel model. Practical implications for designing grade-differentiated educational AI products are discussed.

items.title: Generative AI in higher education: A scoping review and framework for student motivation and engagement
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly influencing how students write, create, reflect, solve problems, and engage with learning in higher education. However, the evidence remains divided, particularly regarding motivation, engagement, creativity, perception, self-regulation, and psychologically informed learning design. This study presents a PRISMA-ScR-based scoping review of GenAI in higher education from a motivational and psychological perspective. The final corpus included 195 studies published between 2023 and 2025 within a specified eligibility window of January 2021 to December 2025. Records were dual screened, coded using a structured framework, and analyzed across psychological focus, thematic constructs, GenAI tools, study designs, outcomes, contextual characteristics, self-determination theory (SDT) needs, equity, and evidence strength. The screening agreement was 81.9%, with Cohen’s κ = 0.642. Motivation was the most common primary focus (31.3%), followed by perception (26.7%), engagement (18.5%), creativity (15.4%), and general/other (8.2%). The literature was dominated by ChatGPT and general GenAI systems, while survey-based and observational evidence was far more common than experimental evidence, longitudinal research, or studies reporting objective performance outcomes. Among 155 empirical studies, mixed or conditional outcomes were most frequent (46.5%), compared with predominantly positive findings (21.9%). SDT related evidence was most common for competence (42.6%), followed by autonomy (29.7%) and relatedness (22.6%), although direct measurement was rare. Based on these findings, the study proposes the GenAI engagement framework, a literature informed structure that organizes five recurring components of GenAI supported learning without assuming a fixed sequence or causal pathway. The framework is not presented as a validated causal model, but as a structured basis for future research and instructional design. The findings suggest that the educational value of GenAI depends less on the technology itself than on how it is guided, evaluated, and integrated into meaningful learning activities.

items.title: Generative AI-assisted learning and perceived academic performance in higher education: the indirect role of self-efficacy and the moderating role of AI literacy
items.abstract: Introduction Generative AI is increasingly used to support learning in higher education, yet the association between generative AI-assisted learning use and students’ perceived academic performance, as well as the conditions under which this association varies, remains unclear. Drawing on social cognitive theory and AI literacy research, this study tested whether generative AI-assisted learning use was indirectly associated with perceived academic performance through self-efficacy and whether AI literacy conditioned the association between generative AI-assisted learning use and self-efficacy. Methods Cross-sectional questionnaire data were collected from 376 undergraduates at universities in China. An item-level latent interaction structural equation was estimated using a matched-pair product-indicator approach. Results The model showed positive associations between generative AI-assisted learning use and self-efficacy ( β = 0.207, p < 0.001) and between self-efficacy and perceived academic performance ( β = 0.199, p < 0.001). The latent interaction between generative AI-assisted learning use and AI literacy was positive ( B = 0.068, 95% bias-corrected bootstrap confidence interval [0.012, 0.123]), indicating that the association between generative AI-assisted learning use and self-efficacy was stronger at higher levels of AI literacy. The conditional indirect association was not statistically significant at low AI literacy but was positive and statistically significant at the mean and high levels. The index of moderated mediation was 0.011 (95% bias-corrected bootstrap confidence interval [0.002, 0.026]), indicating that the indirect association varied across levels of AI literacy. Discussion These findings describe a theory-consistent conditional pattern of cross-sectional associations but do not establish temporal or causal ordering.

items.title: Generative LLM for adaptive taxonomy-informed multi-label classification in construction safety
items.abstract: Accurate hierarchical multi-label classification of construction accident narratives is vital, yet traditional methods struggle with the Occupational Injury and Illness Classification System (OIICS), which contains over 2000 labels across four attributes with four-level hierarchies and is subject to taxonomic updates. This paper proposes the Adaptive Generative Construction Classification (AGCC), a taxonomy-informed generative framework that reformulates coding as structured sequence-to-sequence generation. Each attribute is predicted at a variable depth using leaf codes, while taxonomy-informed serialization and semantic-aware label verbalization promote hierarchical consistency. AGCC incorporates Low-Rank Adaptation for parameter-efficient fine-tuning. On OIICS 3.0, AGCC achieves 74.36% Weighted-F1 (Flat) and 84.66% Weighted-F1 (Hierarchical), outperforming full fine-tuning of FLAN-T5-Large by 4.41 and 2.74 percentage points, respectively. Macro-F1 improves by 5.78 and 5.53 percentage points, respectively, while 3.2% of parameters are trainable. AGCC transfers across backbones and demonstrates robustness to taxonomy shifts, offering an accurate and scalable solution for construction safety coding under evolving taxonomies.

items.title: Geospatial Education at the GIS–GeoAI Interface: A PRISMA-Guided Bibliometric Mapping of a Scopus Corpus, 2002–2025
items.abstract: Geospatial information is used in education as disciplinary content and as a learning technology, while computational geospatial research increasingly employs artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, and remote sensing. This study maps the publication performance and thematic structure of a broad Scopus corpus at the interface of geospatial technology and education from 2002 to 2025. A PRISMA-guided review and bibliometric analysis were conducted on 125 documents from 68 sources using bibliometrix and Biblioshiny in R. The corpus showed an annual publication growth rate of 10.99%, an average of 11.93 citations per document, and 2.81 authors per document. The Journal of Geography was the most productive source, while De Lázaro-Torres and De Miguel González were the most productive authors. Co-word analysis identified an educational GIS cluster, a geospatial technology and learning cluster, and a computational geospatial cluster containing GeoAI-related terms. The increased visibility of the computational cluster in 2022–2025 indicates an emerging thematic orientation, not evidence that GeoAI has replaced GIS-based education or already dominates educational practice. Because the search expression included the broad term learning and the corpus retained several technical geospatial records, the findings should be interpreted as an exploratory map of the education–technology interface. The proposed instructional sequence is therefore a theory-informed research proposition that requires empirical validation
